M3 · Angular Momentum Algebra

Part 0 — Foundations · Status: draft v1 · Companion notebook: M3_angular_momentum.ipynb

Learning goals. After this chapter you should be able to

  • derive the spectrum of angular momentum from the commutation relations, and build the matrices of
    J\mathbf JJ for any jjj;
  • describe orbital angular momentum, parity and spin ½, including the sign change of a spinor under a
    rotation by 2π2\pi2π;
  • couple two angular momenta with Clebsch–Gordan coefficients and 3j symbols, and explain their
    semiclassical meaning;
  • explain how the spin–orbit interaction splits single-particle levels and produces the nuclear magic
    numbers;
  • rotate states and operators with Wigner DDD-matrices, and describe a deformed nucleus in the
    laboratory frame;
  • reduce matrix elements of tensor operators with the Wigner–Eckart theorem, and use it for
    quadrupole moments and B(E2)B(E2)B(E2) values;
  • recouple three and four angular momenta with 6j and 9j symbols, and compute the coupling matrix of
    a deformed potential;
  • list the coupled channels of a reaction for a given total JπJ^\piJπ.

Prerequisites: M1 (spherical harmonics and
Legendre polynomials). A first course in quantum mechanics helps but is not required.

Sources: C&H §6.1 (collisions of particles with spin) and §9.3 (partial-wave expansions with spin
in coupled channels); Thompson (1988), Appendix A (notation and phase conventions); Edmonds (1957) and
Brink & Satchler (1993) for the formulas of angular-momentum algebra; Bohr & Mottelson, Vol. I, for
the single-particle potential.

How to read this chapter. Scattering problems with spins or with excited states of the nuclei
are bookkeeping problems in angular momentum. This chapter collects the tools: Sections M3.1–M3.4
build them, M3.5–M3.7 apply them to single-particle levels and deformed nuclei, and M3.8–M3.9
assemble the coupled-channel basis of Chapters 6, 9 and 14. The notebook checks every formula
against exact values from sympy or by brute-force sums, and the tools live in scatlib.angmom.

M3.1 Angular momentum operators and eigenstates

Any three operators JxJ_xJx​, JyJ_yJy​, JzJ_zJz​ that obey

[Jx,Jy]=iℏJz,[Jy,Jz]=iℏJx,[Jz,Jx]=iℏJy(M3.1)[J_x, J_y] = i\hbar J_z,\qquad [J_y, J_z] = i\hbar J_x,\qquad [J_z, J_x] = i\hbar J_y \tag{M3.1} [Jx​,Jy​]=iℏJz​,[Jy​,Jz​]=iℏJx​,[Jz​,Jx​]=iℏJy​(M3.1)

are an angular momentum: orbital angular momentum L=r×p\mathbf L = \mathbf r\times\mathbf pL=r×p, spin, and
their sums. The commutation relations alone fix the spectrum. From here on we set ℏ=1\hbar = 1ℏ=1 in
angular-momentum algebra.

The spectrum. J2\mathbf J^2J2 commutes with every component, so J2\mathbf J^2J2 and JzJ_zJz​ have common
eigenstates. Define the ladder operators J±=Jx±iJyJ_\pm = J_x \pm iJ_yJ±​=Jx​±iJy​. By (M3.1),
[Jz,J±]=±J±[J_z, J_\pm] = \pm J_\pm[Jz​,J±​]=±J±​, so J±J_\pmJ±​ raises or lowers the eigenvalue of JzJ_zJz​ by one and leaves
J2\mathbf J^2J2 alone. Since J∓J±=J2−Jz2∓JzJ_\mp J_\pm = \mathbf J^2 - J_z^2 \mp J_zJ∓​J±​=J2−Jz2​∓Jz​, the squared norm of
J±∣λm⟩J_\pm|\lambda m\rangleJ±​∣λm⟩ is λ−m(m±1)\lambda - m(m \pm 1)λ−m(m±1), which cannot be negative. The ladder must
therefore stop at both ends. If jjj is the largest mmm, then J+∣λj⟩=0J_+|\lambda j\rangle = 0J+​∣λj⟩=0 gives
λ=j(j+1)\lambda = j(j+1)λ=j(j+1), and the smallest mmm is −j-j−j. Going from jjj to −j-j−j in integer steps requires
2j2j2j to be an integer. Hence

J2∣jm⟩=j(j+1) ∣jm⟩,Jz∣jm⟩=m ∣jm⟩,j=0,12,1,32,…,m=−j,−j+1,…,j,(M3.2)\mathbf J^2|jm\rangle = j(j+1)\,|jm\rangle,\qquad J_z|jm\rangle = m\,|jm\rangle,\qquad j = 0, \tfrac12, 1, \tfrac32, \dots,\quad m = -j, -j+1, \dots, j , \tag{M3.2} J2∣jm⟩=j(j+1)∣jm⟩,Jz​∣jm⟩=m∣jm⟩,j=0,21​,1,23​,…,m=−j,−j+1,…,j,(M3.2)

and the ladder operators act as

J±∣jm⟩=j(j+1)−m(m±1)  ∣j,m±1⟩.(M3.3)J_\pm|jm\rangle = \sqrt{j(j+1) - m(m\pm1)}\;|j,m\pm1\rangle . \tag{M3.3} J±​∣jm⟩=j(j+1)−m(m±1)​∣j,m±1⟩.(M3.3)

The phase of (M3.3), real and positive, is the Condon–Shortley convention, used everywhere in
these notes. Equation (M3.3) gives the matrices of Jx=(J++J−)/2J_x = (J_+ + J_-)/2Jx​=(J+​+J−​)/2 and Jy=(J+−J−)/2iJ_y = (J_+ - J_-)/2iJy​=(J+​−J−​)/2i for
any jjj; scatlib.angmom.jmatrices builds them, and the notebook confirms (M3.1) and (M3.2) to
10−1410^{-14}10−14 for jjj up to 15/215/215/2.

The vector model. In the state ∣jm⟩|jm\rangle∣jm⟩,

⟨Jx2⟩=⟨Jy2⟩=12[j(j+1)−m2]>0.(M3.4)\langle J_x^2\rangle = \langle J_y^2\rangle = \tfrac12\big[j(j+1) - m^2\big] > 0 . \tag{M3.4} ⟨Jx2​⟩=⟨Jy2​⟩=21​[j(j+1)−m2]>0.(M3.4)

Even for m=jm = jm=j the transverse components do not vanish: an angular momentum never points exactly
along an axis. Semiclassically, J\mathbf JJ has length j(j+1)\sqrt{j(j+1)}j(j+1)​ and lies on a cone about the
zzz axis with cos⁡θ=m/j(j+1)\cos\theta = m/\sqrt{j(j+1)}cosθ=m/j(j+1)​; for j=2j = 2j=2, m=2m = 2m=2 the half-angle of the cone is
35.3°. This picture will explain the Clebsch–Gordan coefficients in §M3.4.

M3.2 Orbital angular momentum and parity

For L=r×p\mathbf L = \mathbf r\times\mathbf pL=r×p, in spherical coordinates, Lz=−i ∂/∂ϕL_z = -i\,\partial/\partial\phiLz​=−i∂/∂ϕ
and L2\mathbf L^2L2 is the angular part of the Laplacian (M1.2). The ladder operators are

L±=e±iϕ(±∂∂θ+icot⁡θ ∂∂ϕ),(M3.5)L_\pm = e^{\pm i\phi}\left(\pm\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta} + i\cot\theta\,\frac{\partial}{\partial\phi}\right), \tag{M3.5} L±​=e±iϕ(±∂θ∂​+icotθ∂ϕ∂​),(M3.5)

and the eigenfunctions are the spherical harmonics Ylm(θ,ϕ)Y_{lm}(\theta, \phi)Ylm​(θ,ϕ) of M1. A wave function must
be single valued, so eimϕe^{im\phi}eimϕ forces integer mmm, and therefore integer lll. Half-integer
angular momenta exist only as spin.

Parity. The parity operator maps r→−r\mathbf r \to -\mathbf rr→−r, that is θ→π−θ\theta \to \pi - \thetaθ→π−θ and
ϕ→ϕ+π\phi \to \phi + \piϕ→ϕ+π. Under it

Ylm(π−θ,ϕ+π)=(−1)l Ylm(θ,ϕ),(M3.6)Y_{lm}(\pi - \theta, \phi + \pi) = (-1)^l\,Y_{lm}(\theta, \phi), \tag{M3.6} Ylm​(π−θ,ϕ+π)=(−1)lYlm​(θ,ϕ),(M3.6)

which the notebook confirms to 4×10−154\times10^{-15}4×10−15 for l≤5l \le 5l≤5. A partial wave lll has parity
(−1)l(-1)^l(−1)l. In a central potential both lll and parity are conserved. In a non-central one, such as the
potential of a deformed nucleus or the tensor force, only the total angular momentum and the parity
survive. That is why reaction channels are labelled by JπJ^\piJπ (§M3.9).

Figure M3.1. The real spherical harmonics Yl0Y_{l0}Yl0​ and 2 Re Ylm\sqrt2\,\mathrm{Re}\,Y_{lm}2​ReYlm​
(∝cos⁡mϕ\propto\cos m\phi∝cosmϕ) for l≤3l \le 3l≤3, drawn as surfaces at distance ∣Y∣|Y|∣Y∣ from the origin and coloured
by sign (red positive, blue negative). Each has mmm nodal planes through the zzz axis and l−ml - ml−m
nodal cones; for odd lll the sign changes under r→−r\mathbf r \to -\mathbf rr→−r. (Notebook §M3.2.)

M3.3 Spin one-half

For j=12j = \frac12j=21​ the angular momentum is S=σ/2\mathbf S = \boldsymbol\sigma/2S=σ/2, with the Pauli matrices
(basis m=+12,−12m = +\frac12, -\frac12m=+21​,−21​)

σx=(0110),σy=(0−ii0),σz=(100−1),σiσj=δij+i ϵijk σk.(M3.7)\sigma_x = \begin{pmatrix}0 & 1\\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_y = \begin{pmatrix}0 & -i\\ i & 0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_z = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\ 0 & -1\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_i\sigma_j = \delta_{ij} + i\,\epsilon_{ijk}\,\sigma_k . \tag{M3.7} σx​=(01​10​),σy​=(0i​−i0​),σz​=(10​0−1​),σi​σj​=δij​+iϵijk​σk​.(M3.7)

(scatlib orders the basis by increasing mmm, so its matrices appear with rows and columns reversed.)
The product rule gives (σ⋅n^)2=1(\boldsymbol\sigma\cdot\hat{\mathbf n})^2 = 1(σ⋅n^)2=1, and a rotation by β\betaβ about
the axis n^\hat{\mathbf n}n^ is

e−iβ σ⋅n^/2=cos⁡β2−i σ⋅n^ sin⁡β2.(M3.8)e^{-i\beta\,\boldsymbol\sigma\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}/2} = \cos\frac{\beta}{2} - i\,\boldsymbol\sigma\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}\,\sin\frac{\beta}{2} . \tag{M3.8} e−iβσ⋅n^/2=cos2β​−iσ⋅n^sin2β​.(M3.8)

At β=2π\beta = 2\piβ=2π this is −1-1−1. A spinor changes sign under a full turn and returns to itself only
after 4π4\pi4π (Fig. M3.4a). Observables are bilinear in the spinor and do not notice. But the sign is
real. In neutron interferometry, one of two coherent beams has its spin precessed in a magnetic field.
The interference pattern is shifted by half a period after a precession of 2π2\pi2π, and repeats only
after 4π4\pi4π (Rauch et al. 1975; Werner et al. 1975).

The state “spin up along n^\hat{\mathbf n}n^”, with polar angles (θ,ϕ)(\theta, \phi)(θ,ϕ), is the eigenvector of
σ⋅n^\boldsymbol\sigma\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}σ⋅n^ with eigenvalue +1+1+1,
χ=(cos⁡θ2, eiϕsin⁡θ2)\chi = \big(\cos\frac\theta2,\ e^{i\phi}\sin\frac\theta2\big)χ=(cos2θ​, eiϕsin2θ​), and its ⟨σ⟩\langle\boldsymbol\sigma\rangle⟨σ⟩
is n^\hat{\mathbf n}n^. Every spin-½ state is spin up along some direction, which is why the polarization
of a spin-½ beam is described by a single vector (Chapter 6).

M3.4 Coupling two angular momenta

Two angular momenta j1\mathbf j_1j1​ and j2\mathbf j_2j2​ acting on different degrees of freedom (orbit and
spin, or two particles) commute, and their sum J=j1+j2\mathbf J = \mathbf j_1 + \mathbf j_2J=j1​+j2​ is again an
angular momentum. Two bases describe the same (2j1+1)(2j2+1)(2j_1+1)(2j_2+1)(2j1​+1)(2j2​+1) states: the product basis
∣j1m1⟩∣j2m2⟩|j_1m_1\rangle|j_2m_2\rangle∣j1​m1​⟩∣j2​m2​⟩, with j1zj_{1z}j1z​ and j2zj_{2z}j2z​ diagonal, and the coupled basis
∣j1j2;JM⟩|j_1j_2;JM\rangle∣j1​j2​;JM⟩, with J2\mathbf J^2J2 and JzJ_zJz​ diagonal. The Clebsch–Gordan coefficients
connect them:

∣j1j2;JM⟩=∑m1m2⟨j1m1j2m2∣JM⟩ ∣j1m1⟩∣j2m2⟩.(M3.9)|j_1j_2;JM\rangle = \sum_{m_1m_2}\langle j_1m_1j_2m_2|JM\rangle\,|j_1m_1\rangle|j_2m_2\rangle . \tag{M3.9} ∣j1​j2​;JM⟩=m1​m2​∑​⟨j1​m1​j2​m2​∣JM⟩∣j1​m1​⟩∣j2​m2​⟩.(M3.9)

They vanish unless M=m1+m2M = m_1 + m_2M=m1​+m2​ and JJJ obeys the triangle rule ∣j1−j2∣≤J≤j1+j2|j_1 - j_2| \le J \le j_1 + j_2∣j1​−j2​∣≤J≤j1​+j2​.
The count works: ∑J(2J+1)=(2j1+1)(2j2+1)\sum_J(2J+1) = (2j_1+1)(2j_2+1)∑J​(2J+1)=(2j1​+1)(2j2​+1).

Construction. Start from the stretched state, ∣J=j1+j2,M=J⟩=∣j1j1⟩∣j2j2⟩|J = j_1+j_2, M = J\rangle = |j_1j_1\rangle|j_2j_2\rangle∣J=j1​+j2​,M=J⟩=∣j1​j1​⟩∣j2​j2​⟩.
Apply J−=j1−+j2−J_- = j_{1-} + j_{2-}J−​=j1−​+j2−​ with (M3.3) to obtain the other members of that multiplet. The state with
M=j1+j2−1M = j_1 + j_2 - 1M=j1​+j2​−1 orthogonal to them starts the multiplet J=j1+j2−1J = j_1 + j_2 - 1J=j1​+j2​−1, and so on. With the
convention that ⟨j1j1 j2(J−j1)∣JJ⟩>0\langle j_1j_1\,j_2(J - j_1)|JJ\rangle > 0⟨j1​j1​j2​(J−j1​)∣JJ⟩>0, all coefficients are real. For l=1l = 1l=1
coupled to spin ½ (a ppp orbit) the notebook prints the exact values:

∣32,12⟩=13 ∣1,−12⟩+23 ∣0,12⟩,∣12,12⟩=23 ∣1,−12⟩−13 ∣0,12⟩,(M3.10)\Big|\tfrac32, \tfrac12\Big\rangle = \sqrt{\tfrac13}\,\Big|1, -\tfrac12\Big\rangle + \sqrt{\tfrac23}\,\Big|0, \tfrac12\Big\rangle,\qquad \Big|\tfrac12, \tfrac12\Big\rangle = \sqrt{\tfrac23}\,\Big|1, -\tfrac12\Big\rangle - \sqrt{\tfrac13}\,\Big|0, \tfrac12\Big\rangle , \tag{M3.10} ∣∣∣∣​23​,21​⟩=31​​∣∣∣∣​1,−21​⟩+32​​∣∣∣∣​0,21​⟩,∣∣∣∣​21​,21​⟩=32​​∣∣∣∣​1,−21​⟩−31​​∣∣∣∣​0,21​⟩,(M3.10)

where ∣ml,ms⟩|m_l, m_s\rangle∣ml​,ms​⟩ on the right denotes the product state. These are the p3/2p_{3/2}p3/2​ and p1/2p_{1/2}p1/2​
states of the shell model.

Orthogonality. Both bases are orthonormal, so the coefficients form a real orthogonal matrix:

∑m1m2⟨j1m1j2m2∣JM⟩⟨j1m1j2m2∣J′M′⟩=δJJ′δMM′,∑JM⟨j1m1j2m2∣JM⟩⟨j1m1′j2m2′∣JM⟩=δm1m1′δm2m2′.(M3.11)\sum_{m_1m_2}\langle j_1m_1j_2m_2|JM\rangle\langle j_1m_1j_2m_2|J'M'\rangle = \delta_{JJ'}\delta_{MM'},\qquad \sum_{JM}\langle j_1m_1j_2m_2|JM\rangle\langle j_1m_1'j_2m_2'|JM\rangle = \delta_{m_1m_1'}\delta_{m_2m_2'} . \tag{M3.11} m1​m2​∑​⟨j1​m1​j2​m2​∣JM⟩⟨j1​m1​j2​m2​∣J′M′⟩=δJJ′​δMM′​,JM∑​⟨j1​m1​j2​m2​∣JM⟩⟨j1​m1′​j2​m2′​∣JM⟩=δm1​m1′​​δm2​m2′​​.(M3.11)

Fig. M3.2a shows the matrix for 32⊗1\frac32\otimes123​⊗1: block diagonal in MMM, and orthogonal to 2×10−162\times10^{-16}2×10−16.

3j symbols. The Wigner 3j symbol has more symmetry:

⟨j1m1j2m2∣JM⟩=(−1)j1−j2+M2J+1(j1j2Jm1m2−M).(M3.12)\langle j_1m_1j_2m_2|JM\rangle = (-1)^{j_1 - j_2 + M}\sqrt{2J+1}\begin{pmatrix}j_1 & j_2 & J\\ m_1 & m_2 & -M\end{pmatrix}. \tag{M3.12} ⟨j1​m1​j2​m2​∣JM⟩=(−1)j1​−j2​+M2J+1​(j1​m1​​j2​m2​​J−M​).(M3.12)

A 3j symbol is unchanged by an even permutation of its columns and multiplied by
(−1)j1+j2+j3(-1)^{j_1+j_2+j_3}(−1)j1​+j2​+j3​ by an odd permutation or by reversing the signs of all mmm. It is given in closed
form by Racah’s formula,

(j1j2j3m1m2m3)=(−1)j1−j2−m3 Δ(j1j2j3)∏i(ji+mi)! (ji−mi)!  ∑k(−1)kk! (j3−j2+k+m1)! (j3−j1+k−m2)! (j1+j2−j3−k)! (j1−k−m1)! (j2−k+m2)!,(M3.13)\begin{pmatrix}j_1 & j_2 & j_3\\ m_1 & m_2 & m_3\end{pmatrix} = (-1)^{j_1 - j_2 - m_3}\,\Delta(j_1j_2j_3) \sqrt{\prod_{i}(j_i + m_i)!\,(j_i - m_i)!}\; \sum_k\frac{(-1)^k}{k!\,(j_3 - j_2 + k + m_1)!\,(j_3 - j_1 + k - m_2)!\,(j_1 + j_2 - j_3 - k)!\,(j_1 - k - m_1)!\,(j_2 - k + m_2)!}, \tag{M3.13} (j1​m1​​j2​m2​​j3​m3​​)=(−1)j1​−j2​−m3​Δ(j1​j2​j3​)i∏​(ji​+mi​)!(ji​−mi​)!​k∑​k!(j3​−j2​+k+m1​)!(j3​−j1​+k−m2​)!(j1​+j2​−j3​−k)!(j1​−k−m1​)!(j2​−k+m2​)!(−1)k​,(M3.13)

with Δ(abc)=(a+b−c)! (a−b+c)! (−a+b+c)!/(a+b+c+1)!\Delta(abc) = \sqrt{(a+b-c)!\,(a-b+c)!\,(-a+b+c)!/(a+b+c+1)!}Δ(abc)=(a+b−c)!(a−b+c)!(−a+b+c)!/(a+b+c+1)!​ and the sum over all kkk for which
the factorials have non-negative arguments. The alternating sum loses digits in floating point for
large quantum numbers. scatlib.angmom therefore evaluates it in exact integer arithmetic and rounds
only at the end. All 2408 coefficients with j1,j2≤3j_1, j_2 \le 3j1​,j2​≤3 agree with the exact sympy values to
2×10−162\times10^{-16}2×10−16.

The semiclassical meaning. Picture j1\mathbf j_1j1​ and j2\mathbf j_2j2​ as vectors of lengths
j~=j+12\tilde j = j + \frac12j~​=j+21​ adding to J\mathbf JJ. With J\mathbf JJ fixed, j1\mathbf j_1j1​ can only
precess uniformly about J\mathbf JJ on a cone. Its projection on J\mathbf JJ is
a=(J~2+j~12−j~22)/2J~a = (\tilde J^2 + \tilde j_1^2 - \tilde j_2^2)/2\tilde Ja=(J~2+j~​12​−j~​22​)/2J~ and the radius of the cone is
b=j~12−a2b = \sqrt{\tilde j_1^2 - a^2}b=j~​12​−a2​. If J\mathbf JJ makes the angle Θ\ThetaΘ with the zzz axis,
cos⁡Θ=M/J~\cos\Theta = M/\tilde JcosΘ=M/J~, then m1=acos⁡Θ+bsin⁡Θcos⁡ψm_1 = a\cos\Theta + b\sin\Theta\cos\psim1​=acosΘ+bsinΘcosψ with ψ\psiψ uniform, and

∣⟨j1m1j2m2∣JM⟩∣2  ≈  P(m1)=1πb2sin⁡2Θ−(m1−acos⁡Θ)2.(M3.14)|\langle j_1m_1j_2m_2|JM\rangle|^2 \;\approx\; P(m_1) = \frac{1}{\pi\sqrt{b^2\sin^2\Theta - (m_1 - a\cos\Theta)^2}} . \tag{M3.14} ∣⟨j1​m1​j2​m2​∣JM⟩∣2≈P(m1​)=πb2sin2Θ−(m1​−acosΘ)2​1​.(M3.14)

M3.5 Spin–orbit coupling

A spin-½ particle in an orbit lll has the coupled states ∣(l12)jm⟩|(l\tfrac12)jm\rangle∣(l21​)jm⟩ with j=l±12j = l \pm \frac12j=l±21​.
Their angular parts are the spin-angle functions

Yjml=∑ms=±1/2⟨l, m−ms, 12, ms∣jm⟩  Yl,m−ms(r^) χms.(M3.15)\mathcal Y^{l}_{jm} = \sum_{m_s = \pm1/2}\big\langle l,\,m - m_s,\,\tfrac12,\,m_s\big|jm\big\rangle\;Y_{l,m-m_s}(\hat{\mathbf r})\,\chi_{m_s} . \tag{M3.15} Yjml​=ms​=±1/2∑​⟨l,m−ms​,21​,ms​∣∣∣​jm⟩Yl,m−ms​​(r^)χms​​.(M3.15)

The operator l⋅s=12(j2−l2−s2)\mathbf l\cdot\mathbf s = \frac12(\mathbf j^2 - \mathbf l^2 - \mathbf s^2)l⋅s=21​(j2−l2−s2) is diagonal in this
basis:

⟨l⋅s⟩=12[j(j+1)−l(l+1)−34]={     l/2,j=l+12,−(l+1)/2,j=l−12.(M3.16)\langle\mathbf l\cdot\mathbf s\rangle = \tfrac12\big[j(j+1) - l(l+1) - \tfrac34\big] = \begin{cases} \;\;\,l/2, & j = l + \frac12,\\ -(l+1)/2, & j = l - \frac12 .\end{cases} \tag{M3.16} ⟨l⋅s⟩=21​[j(j+1)−l(l+1)−43​]={l/2,−(l+1)/2,​j=l+21​,j=l−21​.​(M3.16)

A spin–orbit interaction therefore splits each orbit l>0l > 0l>0 into two levels, and the splitting grows
like (2l+1)/2(2l+1)/2(2l+1)/2.

The nuclear spin–orbit potential. In nuclei the spin–orbit force is strong, peaked at the surface,
and of the opposite sign to the atomic one: the level with j=l+12j = l + \frac12j=l+21​ lies lower. A standard
single-particle potential (Bohr & Mottelson) is

V(r)=V0 f(r)+Vls r02 1rdfdr ⟨l⋅s⟩,f(r)=11+e(r−R)/a,(M3.17)V(r) = V_0\,f(r) + V_{ls}\,r_0^2\,\frac{1}{r}\frac{df}{dr}\,\langle\mathbf l\cdot\mathbf s\rangle,\qquad f(r) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{(r - R)/a}}, \tag{M3.17} V(r)=V0​f(r)+Vls​r02​r1​drdf​⟨l⋅s⟩,f(r)=1+e(r−R)/a1​,(M3.17)

with V0=−51+33(N−Z)/AV_0 = -51 + 33(N - Z)/AV0​=−51+33(N−Z)/A MeV for neutrons, Vls=−0.44 V0V_{ls} = -0.44\,V_0Vls​=−0.44V0​, R=r0A1/3R = r_0A^{1/3}R=r0​A1/3,
r0=1.27r_0 = 1.27r0​=1.27 fm and a=0.67a = 0.67a=0.67 fm. Since df/dr<0df/dr < 0df/dr<0, the spin–orbit term is attractive for
j=l+12j = l + \frac12j=l+21​. For the neutrons of ²⁰⁸Pb, V0=−44.02V_0 = -44.02V0​=−44.02 MeV, Vls=19.37V_{ls} = 19.37Vls​=19.37 MeV and
R=7.525R = 7.525R=7.525 fm.

The notebook finds the bound levels of (M3.17) with the bound-state solver of Chapter 2, while the
spin–orbit strength is turned on from zero to its full value (Fig. M3.3 and Animation M3.2). Without
spin–orbit coupling, the wide gaps fall at N=2,8,20,40,58,92N = 2, 8, 20, 40, 58, 92N=2,8,20,40,58,92 and 138138138, with weaker ones at
18, 34, 70 and 112. These are the closed shells of a flat-bottomed well, and apart from 2, 8 and 20
they are not the observed magic numbers. With full spin–orbit coupling, the gaps fall at
N=2,8,20,28,50,82N = 2, 8, 20, 28, 50, 82N=2,8,20,28,50,82 and 126126126, with weaker ones at 40 and 100. The decisive levels are the
high-jjj partners 1f7/21f_{7/2}1f7/2​, 1g9/21g_{9/2}1g9/2​, 1h11/21h_{11/2}1h11/2​, 1i13/21i_{13/2}1i13/2​ and 1j15/21j_{15/2}1j15/2​. Each is pulled down
into the shell below, and each creates a new magic number. This explanation of the magic numbers by
Mayer and by Haxel, Jensen and Suess (1949) established the nuclear shell model. Note also the 1j15/21j_{15/2}1j15/2​ level:
it is not bound at all without spin–orbit coupling and becomes bound only above about half strength.

The comparison with experiment is quantitative. The last occupied neutron orbit of ²⁰⁸Pb is
3p1/23p_{1/2}3p1/2​, and its energy is minus the neutron separation energy of ²⁰⁸Pb. The first empty orbit is
2g9/22g_{9/2}2g9/2​, whose energy is minus the separation energy of ²⁰⁹Pb. From the AME2020 masses,
Sn(208Pb)=7.368S_n(^{208}\mathrm{Pb}) = 7.368Sn​(208Pb)=7.368 MeV and Sn(209Pb)=3.937S_n(^{209}\mathrm{Pb}) = 3.937Sn​(209Pb)=3.937 MeV, so the N=126N = 126N=126 gap is
3.43 MeV. The potential gives E(3p1/2)=−7.18E(3p_{1/2}) = -7.18E(3p1/2​)=−7.18 MeV, E(2g9/2)=−3.62E(2g_{9/2}) = -3.62E(2g9/2​)=−3.62 MeV and a gap of
3.55 MeV.

Bold numbers mark the neutron number NNN (states counted with weight 2j+12j+12j+1) at every gap wider than

In reactions. The same surface-peaked form appears in the optical potential, where it produces
the polarization of scattered nucleons (Chapter 6). Bound states of (M3.17) are the form factors of
transfer reactions (Chapters 11–12). Optical-model codes usually write the term in the Thomas form,
with (ℏ/mπc)2≈2.0(\hbar/m_\pi c)^2 \approx 2.0(ℏ/mπ​c)2≈2.0 fm² in place of r02r_0^2r02​, and often with
l⋅σ=2 l⋅s\mathbf l\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma = 2\,\mathbf l\cdot\mathbf sl⋅σ=2l⋅s. In that form the strength above
corresponds to Vso≈7.8V_{so} \approx 7.8Vso​≈7.8 MeV, a typical optical-model value. Always check a code’s
convention before copying parameters; for FRESCO, see Thompson’s manual.

M3.6 Rotation matrices

A rotation by the Euler angles (α,β,γ)(\alpha, \beta, \gamma)(α,β,γ) is: first by γ\gammaγ about zzz, then by
β\betaβ about yyy, then by α\alphaα about zzz. Its operator is
R(α,β,γ)=e−iαJze−iβJye−iγJzR(\alpha, \beta, \gamma) = e^{-i\alpha J_z}e^{-i\beta J_y}e^{-i\gamma J_z}R(α,β,γ)=e−iαJz​e−iβJy​e−iγJz​. A rotation commutes with
J2\mathbf J^2J2, so it never changes jjj, only mixes mmm:

R ∣jm⟩=∑m′∣jm′⟩ Dm′mj(α,β,γ),Dm′mj(α,β,γ)=e−im′α dm′mj(β) e−imγ.(M3.18)R\,|jm\rangle = \sum_{m'}|jm'\rangle\,D^j_{m'm}(\alpha, \beta, \gamma),\qquad D^j_{m'm}(\alpha, \beta, \gamma) = e^{-im'\alpha}\,d^j_{m'm}(\beta)\,e^{-im\gamma} . \tag{M3.18} R∣jm⟩=m′∑​∣jm′⟩Dm′mj​(α,β,γ),Dm′mj​(α,β,γ)=e−im′αdm′mj​(β)e−imγ.(M3.18)

The reduced rotation matrices dm′mj(β)=⟨jm′∣e−iβJy∣jm⟩d^j_{m'm}(\beta) = \langle jm'|e^{-i\beta J_y}|jm\rangledm′mj​(β)=⟨jm′∣e−iβJy​∣jm⟩ are real and
given by Wigner’s formula:

dm′mj(β)=∑k(−1)k−m+m′(j+m)! (j−m)! (j+m′)! (j−m′)!(j+m−k)! k! (j−k−m′)! (k−m+m′)!(cos⁡β2)2j−2k+m−m′(sin⁡β2)2k−m+m′.(M3.19)d^j_{m'm}(\beta) = \sum_k\frac{(-1)^{k - m + m'}\sqrt{(j+m)!\,(j-m)!\,(j+m')!\,(j-m')!}} {(j + m - k)!\,k!\,(j - k - m')!\,(k - m + m')!} \left(\cos\frac\beta2\right)^{2j - 2k + m - m'}\left(\sin\frac\beta2\right)^{2k - m + m'} . \tag{M3.19} dm′mj​(β)=k∑​(j+m−k)!k!(j−k−m′)!(k−m+m′)!(−1)k−m+m′(j+m)!(j−m)!(j+m′)!(j−m′)!​​(cos2β​)2j−2k+m−m′(sin2β​)2k−m+m′.(M3.19)

The DDD-matrices are unitary and multiply like the rotations themselves,
Dj(R1) Dj(R2)=Dj(R1R2)D^j(R_1)\,D^j(R_2) = D^j(R_1R_2)Dj(R1​)Dj(R2​)=Dj(R1​R2​). Their symmetries include
dm′mj(β)=(−1)m−m′dmm′j(β)=d−m,−m′j(β)d^j_{m'm}(\beta) = (-1)^{m - m'}d^j_{mm'}(\beta) = d^j_{-m,-m'}(\beta)dm′mj​(β)=(−1)m−m′dmm′j​(β)=d−m,−m′j​(β). For j=12j = \frac12j=21​, (M3.19) gives
d±1/2,±1/21/2=cos⁡β2d^{1/2}_{\pm1/2,\pm1/2} = \cos\frac\beta2d±1/2,±1/21/2​=cos2β​ and d±1/2,∓1/21/2=∓sin⁡β2d^{1/2}_{\pm1/2,\mp1/2} = \mp\sin\frac\beta2d±1/2,∓1/21/2​=∓sin2β​, which is
(M3.8) again. For integer j=lj = lj=l and m=0m = 0m=0, the rotation matrix is a spherical harmonic:

Dm0l(α,β,γ)=4π2l+1  Ylm∗(β,α),d002=P2(cos⁡β),d102=−32sin⁡βcos⁡β,d202=38sin⁡2β.(M3.20)D^l_{m0}(\alpha, \beta, \gamma) = \sqrt{\frac{4\pi}{2l+1}}\;Y^*_{lm}(\beta, \alpha),\qquad d^2_{00} = P_2(\cos\beta),\quad d^2_{10} = -\sqrt{\tfrac32}\sin\beta\cos\beta,\quad d^2_{20} = \sqrt{\tfrac38}\sin^2\beta . \tag{M3.20} Dm0l​(α,β,γ)=2l+14π​​Ylm∗​(β,α),d002​=P2​(cosβ),d102​=−23​​sinβcosβ,d202​=83​​sin2β.(M3.20)

M3.7 Tensor operators and the Wigner–Eckart theorem

A spherical tensor operator of rank kkk is a set of 2k+12k+12k+1 operators TqkT^k_qTqk​, q=−k,…,kq = -k, \dots, kq=−k,…,k,
that rotate like the spherical harmonics YkqY_{kq}Ykq​:

R Tqk R†=∑q′Tq′k Dq′qk(R),equivalently[Jz,Tqk]=q Tqk,[J±,Tqk]=k(k+1)−q(q±1)  Tq±1k.(M3.23)R\,T^k_q\,R^\dagger = \sum_{q'}T^k_{q'}\,D^k_{q'q}(R),\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad [J_z, T^k_q] = q\,T^k_q,\quad [J_\pm, T^k_q] = \sqrt{k(k+1) - q(q\pm1)}\;T^k_{q\pm1} . \tag{M3.23} RTqk​R†=q′∑​Tq′k​Dq′qk​(R),equivalently[Jz​,Tqk​]=qTqk​,[J±​,Tqk​]=k(k+1)−q(q±1)​Tq±1k​.(M3.23)

Examples are a scalar (k=0k = 0k=0), the spherical components of a vector,
V±1=∓(Vx±iVy)/2V_{\pm1} = \mp(V_x \pm iV_y)/\sqrt2V±1​=∓(Vx​±iVy​)/2​ and V0=VzV_0 = V_zV0​=Vz​ (k=1k = 1k=1), the functions Ykq(r^)Y_{kq}(\hat{\mathbf r})Ykq​(r^)
themselves, the electric multipole operators e rλYλμe\,r^\lambda Y_{\lambda\mu}erλYλμ​, and the quadrupole operator
Q2μ=16π/5 r2Y2μQ_{2\mu} = \sqrt{16\pi/5}\,r^2Y_{2\mu}Q2μ​=16π/5​r2Y2μ​.

The Wigner–Eckart theorem. The dependence of a matrix element of a tensor operator on the
magnetic quantum numbers is pure geometry:

⟨j′m′∣Tqk∣jm⟩=(−1)j′−m′(j′kj−m′qm)⟨j′∥Tk∥j⟩=⟨jm kq∣j′m′⟩2j′+1 ⟨j′∥Tk∥j⟩.(M3.24)\langle j'm'|T^k_q|jm\rangle = (-1)^{j'-m'}\begin{pmatrix}j' & k & j\\ -m' & q & m\end{pmatrix}\langle j'\|T^k\|j\rangle = \frac{\langle jm\,kq|j'm'\rangle}{\sqrt{2j'+1}}\,\langle j'\|T^k\|j\rangle . \tag{M3.24} ⟨j′m′∣Tqk​∣jm⟩=(−1)j′−m′(j′−m′​kq​jm​)⟨j′∥Tk∥j⟩=2j′+1​⟨jmkq∣j′m′⟩​⟨j′∥Tk∥j⟩.(M3.24)

The two forms are equal for integer kkk. All the physics is in one number, the reduced matrix
element ⟨j′∥Tk∥j⟩\langle j'\|T^k\|j\rangle⟨j′∥Tk∥j⟩. The 3j symbol carries the selection rules: m′=m+qm' = m + qm′=m+q and
the triangle ∣j−k∣≤j′≤j+k|j - k| \le j' \le j + k∣j−k∣≤j′≤j+k. A tensor of rank kkk “carries” angular momentum kkk, and its
matrix elements behave like the Clebsch–Gordan coefficients for adding kkk to jjj.

Conventions. (M3.24) follows Edmonds (1957) and Bohr & Mottelson, as do these notes. Other
books absorb the factor 1/2j′+11/\sqrt{2j'+1}1/2j′+1​ into the reduced matrix element, or use a different phase.
Formulas that contain reduced matrix elements, such as B(Eλ)B(E\lambda)B(Eλ) below, then change by such
factors. Always check the convention of a table or a code before using its numbers.

For spherical harmonics, the integral of three of them (the Gaunt integral) gives the reduced
matrix element directly:

∫Yl1m1Yl2m2Yl3m3 dΩ=(2l1+1)(2l2+1)(2l3+1)4π(l1l2l3000)(l1l2l3m1m2m3),⟨l′∥Yλ∥l⟩=(−1)l′(2l′+1)(2λ+1)(2l+1)4π(l′λl000).(M3.25)\int Y_{l_1m_1}Y_{l_2m_2}Y_{l_3m_3}\,d\Omega = \sqrt{\frac{(2l_1+1)(2l_2+1)(2l_3+1)}{4\pi}} \begin{pmatrix}l_1 & l_2 & l_3\\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}l_1 & l_2 & l_3\\ m_1 & m_2 & m_3\end{pmatrix},\qquad \langle l'\|Y_\lambda\|l\rangle = (-1)^{l'}\sqrt{\frac{(2l'+1)(2\lambda+1)(2l+1)}{4\pi}} \begin{pmatrix}l' & \lambda & l\\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}. \tag{M3.25} ∫Yl1​m1​​Yl2​m2​​Yl3​m3​​dΩ=4π(2l1​+1)(2l2​+1)(2l3​+1)​​(l1​0​l2​0​l3​0​)(l1​m1​​l2​m2​​l3​m3​​),⟨l′∥Yλ​∥l⟩=(−1)l′4π(2l′+1)(2λ+1)(2l+1)​​(l′0​λ0​l0​).(M3.25)

The 3j symbol with all m=0m = 0m=0 vanishes unless l1+l2+l3l_1 + l_2 + l_3l1​+l2​+l3​ is even: parity. A multipole
YλY_\lambdaYλ​ connects lll and l′l'l′ only if l+λ+l′l + \lambda + l'l+λ+l′ is even.

computed by numerical quadrature on the sphere. Divided by the geometric factor of (M3.24), the 27
with a non-zero 3j symbol all give the same number, −0.861813824304-0.861813824304−0.861813824304, to 4×10−144\times10^{-14}4×10−14. That is

usually obtained.

M3.8 Recoupling: 6j and 9j symbols

Three angular momenta can be coupled to a total JJJ in different orders: (j1j2)J12(j_1j_2)J_{12}(j1​j2​)J12​ first and then
j3j_3j3​, or (j2j3)J23(j_2j_3)J_{23}(j2​j3​)J23​ first and then j1j_1j1​. Both orders give orthonormal bases. The
transformation between them depends only on angular momenta, not on any mmm, and defines the
Wigner 6j symbol:

⟨(j1j2)J12, j3; J ∣ j1, (j2j3)J23; J⟩=(−1)j1+j2+j3+J(2J12+1)(2J23+1){j1j2J12j3JJ23}.(M3.29)\big\langle (j_1j_2)J_{12},\,j_3;\,J\,\big|\,j_1,\,(j_2j_3)J_{23};\,J\big\rangle = (-1)^{j_1+j_2+j_3+J}\sqrt{(2J_{12}+1)(2J_{23}+1)} \begin{Bmatrix}j_1 & j_2 & J_{12}\\ j_3 & J & J_{23}\end{Bmatrix}. \tag{M3.29} ⟨(j1​j2​)J12​,j3​;J∣∣∣​j1​,(j2​j3​)J23​;J⟩=(−1)j1​+j2​+j3​+J(2J12​+1)(2J23​+1)​{j1​j3​​j2​J​J12​J23​​}.(M3.29)

A 6j symbol vanishes unless its four triads (j1j2J12)(j_1j_2J_{12})(j1​j2​J12​), (j1JJ23)(j_1JJ_{23})(j1​JJ23​), (j3j2J23)(j_3j_2J_{23})(j3​j2​J23​) and
(j3JJ12)(j_3JJ_{12})(j3​JJ12​) satisfy the triangle rule. It is invariant under any permutation of its columns and
under exchanging the upper and lower entries in any two columns. Because (M3.29) is an orthogonal
transformation,

∑J12(2J12+1)(2J23+1){j1j2J12j3JJ23}{j1j2J12j3JJ23′}=δJ23J23′.(M3.30)\sum_{J_{12}}(2J_{12}+1)(2J_{23}+1) \begin{Bmatrix}j_1 & j_2 & J_{12}\\ j_3 & J & J_{23}\end{Bmatrix} \begin{Bmatrix}j_1 & j_2 & J_{12}\\ j_3 & J & J'_{23}\end{Bmatrix} = \delta_{J_{23}J'_{23}} . \tag{M3.30} J12​∑​(2J12​+1)(2J23​+1){j1​j3​​j2​J​J12​J23​​}{j1​j3​​j2​J​J12​J23′​​}=δJ23​J23′​​.(M3.30)

Racah’s formula for the 6j symbol is again an alternating sum of factorials, and scatlib.angmom
again evaluates it exactly.

Two coupling orders for reaction channels. A projectile of spin sss in an orbit lll about a target
of spin III can be coupled in two standard ways (§M3.9). The channel-spin order couples
S=s⊕IS = s \oplus IS=s⊕I first and then J=l⊕SJ = l \oplus SJ=l⊕S. The order used by FRESCO couples j=l⊕sj = l \oplus sj=l⊕s
first and then J=j⊕IJ = j \oplus IJ=j⊕I. By (M3.29),

⟨(ls)j, I; J ∣ l, (sI)S; J⟩=(−1)l+s+I+J(2j+1)(2S+1){lsjIJS}.(M3.31)\big\langle (ls)j,\,I;\,J\,\big|\,l,\,(sI)S;\,J\big\rangle = (-1)^{l+s+I+J}\sqrt{(2j+1)(2S+1)}\begin{Bmatrix}l & s & j\\ I & J & S\end{Bmatrix}. \tag{M3.31} ⟨(ls)j,I;J∣∣∣​l,(sI)S;J⟩=(−1)l+s+I+J(2j+1)(2S+1)​{lI​sJ​jS​}.(M3.31)

For l=2l = 2l=2, s=12s = \frac12s=21​, I=32I = \frac32I=23​ and J=2J = 2J=2, the notebook gets the 2×22\times22×2 matrix with
rows j=32,52j = \frac32, \frac52j=23​,25​ and columns S=1,2S = 1, 2S=1,2:
(−0.5480.8370.8370.548)\begin{pmatrix}-0.548 & 0.837\\ 0.837 & 0.548\end{pmatrix}(−0.5480.837​0.8370.548​). It agrees to 10−1610^{-16}10−16 with the overlaps
of the two bases built explicitly from Clebsch–Gordan coefficients. Cross sections do not depend on
the order, but SSS-matrix elements quoted by different codes do.

9j symbols. Four angular momenta give the 9j symbol. Its main use is the transformation from
LSLSLS coupling (orbital angular momenta coupled to LLL, spins to SSS) to jjjjjj coupling (each particle’s
lll and sss coupled to jjj):

⟨(l1s1)j1, (l2s2)j2; J ∣ (l1l2)L, (s1s2)S; J⟩=(2j1+1)(2j2+1)(2L+1)(2S+1){l1s1j1l2s2j2LSJ},(M3.32)\big\langle (l_1s_1)j_1,\,(l_2s_2)j_2;\,J\,\big|\,(l_1l_2)L,\,(s_1s_2)S;\,J\big\rangle = \sqrt{(2j_1+1)(2j_2+1)(2L+1)(2S+1)} \begin{Bmatrix}l_1 & s_1 & j_1\\ l_2 & s_2 & j_2\\ L & S & J\end{Bmatrix}, \tag{M3.32} ⟨(l1​s1​)j1​,(l2​s2​)j2​;J∣∣∣​(l1​l2​)L,(s1​s2​)S;J⟩=(2j1​+1)(2j2​+1)(2L+1)(2S+1)​⎩⎪⎨⎪⎧​l1​l2​L​s1​s2​S​j1​j2​J​⎭⎪⎬⎪⎫​,(M3.32)

{j1j2j3j4j5j6j7j8j9}=∑x(−1)2x(2x+1){j1j4j7j8j9x}{j2j5j8j4xj6}{j3j6j9xj1j2}.(M3.33)\begin{Bmatrix}j_1 & j_2 & j_3\\ j_4 & j_5 & j_6\\ j_7 & j_8 & j_9\end{Bmatrix} = \sum_x(-1)^{2x}(2x+1) \begin{Bmatrix}j_1 & j_4 & j_7\\ j_8 & j_9 & x\end{Bmatrix} \begin{Bmatrix}j_2 & j_5 & j_8\\ j_4 & x & j_6\end{Bmatrix} \begin{Bmatrix}j_3 & j_6 & j_9\\ x & j_1 & j_2\end{Bmatrix}. \tag{M3.33} ⎩⎪⎨⎪⎧​j1​j4​j7​​j2​j5​j8​​j3​j6​j9​​⎭⎪⎬⎪⎫​=x∑​(−1)2x(2x+1){j1​j8​​j4​j9​​j7​x​}{j2​j4​​j5​x​j8​j6​​}{j3​x​j6​j1​​j9​j2​​}.(M3.33)

For a proton and a neutron in ppp orbits coupled to J=1J = 1J=1, for example, the jjjjjj state
(p1/2)J=12(p_{1/2})^2_{J=1}(p1/2​)J=12​ is −0.19 3S1+0.47 1P1+0.86 3D1-0.19\,{}^3S_1 + 0.47\,{}^1P_1 + 0.86\,{}^3D_1−0.193S1​+0.471P1​+0.863D1​ in LSLSLS coupling. The notebook
prints the full 4×44\times44×4 orthogonal matrix.

Matrix elements of coupled operators. The most important application in reaction theory is the
matrix element of a scalar product of two tensors, TλT^\lambdaTλ acting on one subsystem and UλU^\lambdaUλ on
the other, between coupled states (Edmonds 7.1.6):

⟨(l′I′)J∣ Tλ⋅Uλ ∣(lI)J⟩=(−1)l+I′+J{JI′l′λlI}⟨l′∥Tλ∥l⟩ ⟨I′∥Uλ∥I⟩,(M3.34)\big\langle (l'I')J\big|\,T^\lambda\cdot U^\lambda\,\big|(lI)J\big\rangle = (-1)^{l+I'+J}\begin{Bmatrix}J & I' & l'\\ \lambda & l & I\end{Bmatrix} \langle l'\|T^\lambda\|l\rangle\,\langle I'\|U^\lambda\|I\rangle, \tag{M3.34} ⟨(l′I′)J∣∣∣​Tλ⋅Uλ∣∣∣​(lI)J⟩=(−1)l+I′+J{Jλ​I′l​l′I​}⟨l′∥Tλ∥l⟩⟨I′∥Uλ∥I⟩,(M3.34)

where Tλ⋅Uλ=∑q(−1)qTqλU−qλT^\lambda\cdot U^\lambda = \sum_q(-1)^qT^\lambda_qU^\lambda_{-q}Tλ⋅Uλ=∑q​(−1)qTqλ​U−qλ​. A deformed potential, expanded in
multipoles about the symmetry axis, is exactly such a sum. By the addition theorem,

V(r,θ′)=∑λVλ(r) Yλ0(θ′)=∑λVλ(r) 4π2λ+1  Yλ(r^)⋅Yλ(e^).(M3.35)V(r, \theta') = \sum_\lambda V_\lambda(r)\,Y_{\lambda0}(\theta') = \sum_\lambda V_\lambda(r)\,\sqrt{\frac{4\pi}{2\lambda+1}}\;Y_\lambda(\hat{\mathbf r})\cdot Y_\lambda(\hat{\mathbf e}) . \tag{M3.35} V(r,θ′)=λ∑​Vλ​(r)Yλ0​(θ′)=λ∑​Vλ​(r)2λ+14π​​Yλ​(r^)⋅Yλ​(e^).(M3.35)

The first factor acts on the relative motion and the second on the rotor states YIM(e^)Y_{IM}(\hat{\mathbf e})YIM​(e^).
(M3.34) with the reduced matrix elements (M3.25) gives the coupling matrix between all channels
(l,I)(l, I)(l,I) of a given JJJ. Fig. M3.6 shows it for α + ²⁰Ne with the 0⁺, 2⁺ and 4⁺ states and Jπ=10+J^\pi = 10^+Jπ=10+.
This is the system of the FRESCO test case lane20, the coupled-channels benchmark of Chapter 9,
which uses the quadrupole coupling only. The 6j formula agrees to
10−1610^{-16}10−16 with an explicit sum over all magnetic quantum numbers. The structure of the matrix is the
selection rules made visible:

  • λ=2\lambda = 2λ=2 connects states with ∣I−I′∣≤2|I - I'| \le 2∣I−I′∣≤2 and changes lll by 0 or ±2\pm2±2;
  • the diagonal element in the 0⁺ channel vanishes (a spherical state has no quadrupole moment), while
    the diagonal elements in the 2⁺ and 4⁺ channels (reorientation) do not;
  • λ=4\lambda = 4λ=4 couples the ground state directly to the 4⁺ state.

Figure M3.6. The geometric coupling factors 4π/(2λ+1) ⟨(l′I′)J∣Yλ⋅Yλ∣(lI)J⟩\sqrt{4\pi/(2\lambda+1)}\,\langle(l'I')J|Y_\lambda\cdot Y_\lambda|(lI)J\rangle4π/(2λ+1)​⟨(l′I′)J∣Yλ​⋅Yλ​∣(lI)J⟩
between the nine channels (Iπ,l)(I^\pi, l)(Iπ,l) of α + ²⁰Ne(0⁺, 2⁺, 4⁺) at Jπ=10+J^\pi = 10^+Jπ=10+, for (a) λ=2\lambda = 2λ=2
and (b) λ=4\lambda = 4λ=4. Multiplied by the radial form factors Vλ(r)V_\lambda(r)Vλ​(r), they are the coupling
potentials of the coupled-channel equations. (Notebook §M3.8.)

M3.9 Counting coupled channels

A channel specifies the internal states of the two nuclei (spins sss and III, parities πa\pi_aπa​ and
πA\pi_AπA​), the orbital angular momentum lll of their relative motion, and how the three are coupled.
The total angular momentum JJJ, its projection MMM and the parity are conserved, with

π=πa πA (−1)l.(M3.36)\pi = \pi_a\,\pi_A\,(-1)^l . \tag{M3.36} π=πa​πA​(−1)l.(M3.36)

The coupled-channel equations therefore split into independent sets, one for each JπJ^\piJπ. Listing
the channels in a set is a matter of the triangle rule and (M3.36). scatlib.angmom.channels does it in
both coupling orders of §M3.8; the counts always agree.

Examples from the notebook.

  • α + ²⁰Ne with the 0⁺, 2⁺, 4⁺ band. Jπ=0+J^\pi = 0^+Jπ=0+ has 3 channels, (0+,l=0)(0^+, l{=}0)(0+,l=0), (2+,2)(2^+, 2)(2+,2) and
    (4+,4)(4^+, 4)(4+,4). Jπ=2+J^\pi = 2^+Jπ=2+ has 7. From J=4J = 4J=4 on, every natural-parity set, π=(−1)J\pi = (-1)^Jπ=(−1)J, has
    9 channels. Unnatural-parity sets, such as 1+1^+1+ with 2 channels or Jπ=10−J^\pi = 10^-Jπ=10− with 6, also exist.
    But the entrance channel, α plus ²⁰Ne in its 0⁺ ground state, has π=(−1)l=(−1)J\pi = (-1)^l = (-1)^Jπ=(−1)l=(−1)J, so they
    are never populated.
  • p + ¹²C with the 0⁺ and 2⁺ states. Jπ=32+J^\pi = \frac32^+Jπ=23​+ has 5 channels, for instance
    (0+,l=2,S=12)(0^+, l{=}2, S{=}\frac12)(0+,l=2,S=21​) in the channel-spin order, or (0+,l=2,j=32)(0^+, l{=}2, j{=}\frac32)(0+,l=2,j=23​) in FRESCO’s.
  • Spin ½ on a spin-0 target with no excited states. For each JJJ there are two channels,
    l=J±12l = J \pm \frac12l=J±21​, but they have opposite parity. Each JπJ^\piJπ set therefore has a single channel.
    This is why the phase shifts δl±\delta_l^\pmδl±​ of Chapter 6 do not mix.

How fast the basis grows. For a K=0K = 0K=0 band 0+,2+,…,Imax⁡0^+, 2^+, \dots, I_{\max}0+,2+,…,Imax​ and natural parity with
J≥Imax⁡J \ge I_{\max}J≥Imax​, the state III contributes the I+1I + 1I+1 values l=J−I,J−I+2,…,J+Il = J - I, J - I + 2, \dots, J + Il=J−I,J−I+2,…,J+I.
The number of channels per JJJ is therefore

Nch=∑I=0,2,…Imax⁡(I+1)=(Imax⁡2+1)2,(M3.37)N_{\rm ch} = \sum_{I = 0, 2, \dots}^{I_{\max}}(I + 1) = \Big(\frac{I_{\max}}{2} + 1\Big)^2 , \tag{M3.37} Nch​=I=0,2,…∑Imax​​(I+1)=(2Imax​​+1)2,(M3.37)

that is 9 for the α + ²⁰Ne band and 49 for a band up to 12⁺ (Fig. M3.7). The work of solving coupled
equations grows like Nch3N_{\rm ch}^3Nch3​. The iso-centrifugal approximation of CCFULL (Chapter 14)
replaces the centrifugal barrier of every channel by that of the entrance channel. The algebra then
decouples, and only one channel per intrinsic state remains: 7 instead of 49, a factor of 343 in work.
For heavy-ion fusion, where many partial waves and many excited states contribute, this is what
makes realistic calculations cheap.

Figure M3.7. (a) Number of channels for α + ²⁰Ne(0⁺, 2⁺, 4⁺) as a function of JJJ, for natural and
unnatural parity, and the three channels of the iso-centrifugal approximation (dashed).
(b) Channels per natural-parity JJJ (J≥Imax⁡J \ge I_{\max}J≥Imax​) for a K=0K = 0K=0 band 0+,2+,…,Imax⁡0^+, 2^+, \dots, I_{\max}0+,2+,…,Imax​:
all channels (M3.37) and the iso-centrifugal count (dashed). (Notebook §M3.9.)

Summary

  • The commutation relations fix the spectrum: j(j+1)j(j+1)j(j+1) with 2j2j2j an integer, and 2j+12j+12j+1 values of mmm
    connected by the ladder operators (M3.3). Orbital angular momentum is integer; half-integers come
    only from spin. An angular momentum never points exactly along an axis.
  • Spin ½ is described by the Pauli matrices. A rotation by 2π2\pi2π changes the sign of a spinor.
  • Clebsch–Gordan coefficients and 3j symbols relate product and coupled bases. They form orthogonal
    matrices, obey the triangle rule, and for large quantum numbers oscillate about the probability
    distribution of the classical vector model.
  • ⟨l⋅s⟩=l/2\langle\mathbf l\cdot\mathbf s\rangle = l/2⟨l⋅s⟩=l/2 or −(l+1)/2-(l+1)/2−(l+1)/2. The strong, surface-peaked nuclear spin–orbit
    force pulls the high-jjj levels into the shell below and produces the magic numbers 28, 50, 82 and
    126; for ²⁰⁸Pb the computed N=126N = 126N=126 gap, 3.55 MeV, compares with 3.43 MeV measured.
  • Rotations mix mmm but never jjj, through the DDD-matrices. Dm0lD^l_{m0}Dm0l​ is a spherical harmonic, and
    DM0ID^I_{M0}DM0I​ is the wave function of a rotating K=0K = 0K=0 nucleus.
  • The Wigner–Eckart theorem separates geometry (a 3j symbol) from physics (a reduced matrix element),
    and gives selection rules, Qs=−I2I+3Q0Q_s = -\frac{I}{2I+3}Q_0Qs​=−2I+3I​Q0​ and the relation between B(E2)B(E2)B(E2) and β2\beta_2β2​.
  • 6j and 9j symbols recouple three and four angular momenta. They give the transformations between
    coupling schemes and the coupling matrix elements of a deformed potential in the channel basis.
  • Channels are grouped by JπJ^\piJπ. From a 0⁺ + 0⁺ entrance channel only natural parity is reached.
    The number of channels grows quickly with the number of excited states, which motivates the
    iso-centrifugal approximation.

    What happens when M=JM = JM=J?

  • In §M3.5, compute the proton levels of ²⁰⁸Pb, with V0=−51−33(N−Z)/AV_0 = -51 - 33(N - Z)/AV0​=−51−33(N−Z)/A MeV and the Coulomb
    potential of a uniformly charged sphere (scatlib.potentials.coulomb_sphere). Where is the Z=82Z = 82Z=82
    gap?
  • In §M3.7, check the Wigner–Eckart theorem for ⟨4m′∣Y3q∣1m⟩\langle 4m'|Y_{3q}|1m\rangle⟨4m′∣Y3q​∣1m⟩. Why do all of these
    vanish when you replace Y3Y_3Y3​ by Y2Y_2Y2​?
  • In §M3.8, add the 6⁺ state of ²⁰Ne and recompute the coupling matrix at J=10J = 10J=10. How many channels
